newsitem.title: USA: Nasdaq hits new record, bonds rebound, dollar surges.
newsitem.headline: Nasdaq hits new record, bonds rebound, dollar surges.

text.p: Stocks ended higher on Tuesday, as technology shares led the Nasdaq composite index to its ninth consecutive record close, and the bond market rebounded from an early sell-off.
The dollar surged above 1.80 marks for the first time in nearly six years but ended lower after German officials repeatedly said the dollar had risen too far.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 52.73 points at 7,975.71, surpassing its July 8 record finish of 7,962.31. Earlier in the session, the blue-chip index was down nearly 45 points.
The Nasdaq index rose 18.23 points to a new high of 1,542.11.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks also set a new high, rising 7.38 points to 925.76, as did the NYSE Composite index, up 2.88 to 480.99.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,504 to 1,345 on heavy volume of 598 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Technology stocks extended their dominance, with Hewlett-Packard Co. ranking as the Dow's strongest component for a third straight day, climbing 3-1/2 to 68-9/16.

Hewlett-Packard's gains again mirrored those among the resurgent technology stocks, where mounting optimism has powered Nasdaq to a string of record highs second only to a 10-session run that ended May 1, 1996.
In the process, investors have largely shaken off the effects of some high-profile earnings warnings early in the second quarter, most notably from Intel Corp.
"There is a growing conviction the group is going to do better earnings-wise later in the year and into 1998," said Al Goldman, an analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
Shortly after the close, Intel reported second-quarter earnings of 92 cents a share, 2 cents higher than First Call's consensus analyst forecast.
The powerhouse performance in the tech sector appeared to breathe new life into suddenly sluggish blue chips, which have tracked sideways since nearing the 8,000 mark early last week.
The Dow also overcame some concerns that the soaring dollar, which has approached six-year highs against the German mark, might eventually erode profits of multinational corporations.
While analysts acknowledged that a high dollar could become a burden at some point, many argued the currency also brought near-term benefits that would offset longer-term profit concerns for stocks.

The dollar initially rose against the German mark, ascending to a peak of 1.8040 marks -- its highest level since August 1991 -- on fresh signs that Europe's proposed single currency will be a weak one. It later retreated to close at 1.7910 marks from 1.7955 late Monday.
However, the dollar rose to 115.45 yen from 114.00.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 4/32, with its yield holding at Monday's close of 6.55 percent.
Forecasts for hot weather and little rain in the Midwest drove corn prices higher on concerns that the dryness will stunt growth this month.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for post-harvest delivery in December closed 7-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $2.56-1/2. Wheat for September delivery rose 2-1/4 cents a bushel to close at $3.38-1/4.

Concerns about hot weather also boosted prices of post-harvest delivery prices of soybeans, with November soybeans closing up 4 cents a bushel at $6.25-3/4. July soybeans closed 8 cents a bushel lower at $8.11.

At the New York Mercantile Exchnage, oil prices rose on supply worries. Crude oil for August delivery ended 68 cents higher at $19.67 a barrel after Occidental Petroleum halted shipments from its Cano Limon field in Colombia. The move followed attacks in the last two weeks by anti-government guerrillas.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,899.3, up 41.9 points or 0.86 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,069.41, down 159.31 points, or 0.79 percent.
